assignment.title: Algebra II Honors — District DOL #2 Review: Absolute Value & 3×3 Systems
assignment.essentialQuestion: How do I show that I can analyze and transform absolute value functions, write and solve absolute value equations and inequalities, and write and solve systems of three linear equations?
assignment.teacherNotes: Built from the DeSoto ISD Algebra II Honors DOL #2 blueprint (SY26-27, 20 items): A2.2A (3), A2.3A (2), A2.3B (2), A2.6C (3), A2.6D (3), A2.6E (3), A2.6F (3). Every standard appears in Classwork, Practice and the DOL. Struck from this DOL and therefore left out: √x, 1/x, x³, ∛x, bˣ and log_b(x) parent functions, asymptotic behavior, and linear-quadratic systems. Warm-Up and Classwork are shared for whole-class discussion; Practice and the DOL readiness check give each student their own version, and every Practice item offers a fresh version on “Request New Question.” Practice 11–13 are Digital SAT-style items from MathMaster’s audited CCMR bank (A2.2A, A2.6E, A2.6F), so an Honors class meets its 15% CCMR share with on-blueprint items. The DOL readiness check mixes DOL-format items (choices built from common misconceptions, griddable numbers) with the solving workspace, so a low score can be recovered after practice before the district DOL.

lessonNotesPdf.title: Algebra II Honors — District DOL #2 Study Guide
lessonNotesPdf.subtitle: Absolute value functions, equations, and inequalities · Systems of three equations
lessonNotesPdf.learningGoal: I can graph and analyze absolute value functions and their transformations, write and solve absolute value equations and inequalities, and write and solve systems of three linear equations.

sections.heading: A2.2A · Key attributes of f(x) = a|x − h| + k
bullets: Vertex (h, k); axis of symmetry x = h (the V is symmetric about it).
a > 0: opens up, minimum k, range [k, ∞). a < 0: opens down, maximum k, range (−∞, k].
Domain is always (−∞, ∞). y-intercept: f(0). x-intercepts: solve f(x) = 0 (0, 1, or 2 of them).
Max/min on a closed interval: evaluate the endpoints and the vertex (if it is inside the interval), then compare.

sections.heading: A2.6C · Transformations of f(x) = |x|
bullets: a·f(x): vertical stretch (|a| > 1) or compression (|a| < 1); a < 0 reflects across the x-axis.
f(bx): horizontal compression by 1/|b|. For |x|, |bx| = |b|·|x|, so it equals a vertical stretch by |b|; f(−x) = f(x).
f(x − c): shifts right c when c > 0, left when c < 0 (x’s lie). f(x) + d: shifts up d, or down when d < 0 (y’s tell the truth).
A point (x, y) on |x| maps to (x + h, a·y + k) on a|x − h| + k.

sections.heading: A2.6D · Formulating absolute value equations
content: Absolute value is distance: |x − c| = d means “x is d units from c.” The center c is the midpoint of the two solutions and d is half the distance between them.

workedExample.title: Worked example
workedExample.problem: A bolt must be 5.5 cm long, give or take 0.05 cm. Write an equation for the shortest and longest bolts.

sections.heading: A2.6E and A2.6F · Solving absolute value equations and inequalities
bullets: Isolate the absolute value first. Dividing an INEQUALITY by a negative reverses the symbol.
|A| = d: d > 0 → A = d or A = −d; d = 0 → one solution; d < 0 → no solution. Check every answer.
|A| < d (or ≤): between — −d < A < d, one interval. |A| > d (or ≥): outside — A < −d or A > d, a union.
|A| < negative → no solution; |A| > negative → all real numbers.
Graph: open circles for < and >, closed for ≤ and ≥; write interval notation with ( ) or [ ] and ∪.

sections.heading: A2.3A and A2.3B · Systems of three linear equations
bullets: Formulate: define x, y, z; write one equation per fact (a total count, a total value, a comparison); put each in standard form Ax + By + Cz = D.
Gaussian elimination: eliminate the same variable from two pairs → solve the 2×2 system → back-substitute → check all three equations.
Substitution: solve one equation for a variable with coefficient ±1 and substitute into the other two.
Technology: write A · X = B and compute X = A⁻¹B (or rref of the augmented matrix). If A has no inverse, the system has no solution or infinitely many.
sections.callout: Translate comparisons carefully: “y is 6 more than x” is y = x + 6, and “twice as many s as c” is s = 2c.

questions.prompt: For $g(x)={{a}}|x {{mh|signed}}| {{k|signed}}$, identify the key attributes of its graph.

answerFields.label: Vertex
Axis of symmetry (an equation)
Range (interval notation)
y-intercept (ordered pair)

hints: Compare g with vertex form a|x − h| + k. The vertex is (h, k), and h has the opposite sign of the number you see inside the bars.
The axis of symmetry is the vertical line through the vertex.
A negative a opens the V downward. For the y-intercept, substitute x = 0.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. In g(x) = a|x − h| + k, what does a negative value of a tell you?

solutionReview.headline: Read the vertex from vertex form, then use the sign of a.
reasoning: g(x) = {{a}}|x {{mh|signed}}| {{k|signed}} has the form a|x - h| + k with h = {{h}} and k = {{k}}, so the vertex is ({{h}}, {{k}}).
The axis of symmetry is the vertical line x = {{h}}.
Because a = {{a}} is negative, the V opens downward: {{k}} is the maximum and the range is (-∞, {{k}}].
solutionReview.commonError: Reading the vertex as ({{mh}}, {{k}}) — the number inside the bars has the opposite sign of h.

questions.prompt: The point $({{px}}, {{py}})$ is on the graph of $f(x)=|x|$. The graph of $f$ is transformed to $g(x)={{a}}|x {{mh|signed}}| {{k|signed}}$. Find the image of that point on the graph of $g$.
hints: x’s lie: the change inside the bars moves x. Add h to the x-coordinate.
y’s tell the truth: multiply the y-coordinate by a, then add k.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Which part of g changes the x-coordinate of a point?
options: Only the number inside the bars
scaffold.correct: Only the number inside the bars

solutionReview.headline: A point (x, y) on f moves to (x + h, a·y + k) on g.
solutionReview.commonError: Moving x the wrong way: inside the bars, x {{mh|signed}} is a shift of {{h}}, not {{mh}}.

questions.prompt: Solve the equation. Isolate the absolute value first, then split it into two equations.
hints: Undo the constant outside the bars first, so the absolute value is alone.
If |A| = d with d > 0, then A = d or A = −d. Solve both equations.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. What should be alone on one side before you split the equation?

solutionReview.headline: Isolate, split, solve, check.
reasoning: Solve: x = {{x2}} or x = {{x1}}. Both are {{d}} units from {{h}}, so both check.
solutionReview.commonError: Splitting before the constant {{k}} is moved, which splits the wrong expression.

questions.prompt: A theater sells adult, student, and child tickets. Let a, s, and c be the numbers of adult, student, and child tickets sold. Write an equation for each statement.

answerFields.label: The theater sold {{N}} tickets in all.
Adult tickets cost ${{pa}}, student tickets cost ${{ps}}, and child tickets cost ${{pc}}. Ticket sales totaled ${{R}}.
The theater sold {{m}} times as many student tickets as child tickets.

hints: One equation counts tickets, one counts dollars, and one compares two kinds of tickets.
“{{m}} times as many student tickets as child tickets”: which group is larger? Multiply the smaller group by {{m}} to make the two sides equal.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. If twice as many student tickets as child tickets were sold, which number is larger?

solutionReview.headline: One equation per fact: a count, a total value, and a comparison.
reasoning: Money: price times count for each kind, added: {{pa}}a + {{ps}}s + {{pc}}c = {{R}}.
Comparison: student tickets are {{m}} times child tickets, so s = {{m}}c.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing {{m}}s = c, which says there are more child tickets than student tickets.

sections.title: Classwork — Guided Review of Every DOL #2 Standard

questions.prompt: The graph of an absolute value function f is shown. Work through its key attributes: the intercepts, the maximum or minimum, the axis of symmetry, where f increases and decreases, and its domain and range.

steps.title: Vertex and symmetry
steps.instruction: Every absolute value graph is a V. Its corner is the vertex (h, k). The vertical line x = h through the vertex is the axis of symmetry: the left and right halves are mirror images.

steps.title: Maximum or minimum
steps.instruction: A V that opens down has its maximum at the vertex; a V that opens up has its minimum there. The maximum or minimum VALUE is the vertex’s y-coordinate.

steps.title: Intercepts
steps.instruction: x-intercepts are where y = 0 (an absolute value graph can have 0, 1, or 2). The y-intercept is where x = 0.

steps.title: Increasing and decreasing
steps.instruction: Read the graph left to right and describe x-values only. The behavior changes at the vertex’s x-coordinate, and the intervals are open there.

steps.title: Domain and range
steps.instruction: Every absolute value function has domain (−∞, ∞). The range starts at the vertex’s y-value: (−∞, k] when the V opens down, [k, ∞) when it opens up.

hints: Start with the vertex. It gives you the axis of symmetry and the highest or lowest point of the graph at once.
Intervals of increase and decrease use x-values; the range uses y-values.
The vertex’s y-value is reached, so the range uses a square bracket there.

solutionReview.headline: Find the vertex first; every other attribute follows from it.
reasoning: The vertex is (−1, 4) and the V opens downward, so f has a maximum value of 4 at x = −1, and the axis of symmetry is x = −1.
f crosses the x-axis at (−3, 0) and (1, 0), each 2 units from the axis, and crosses the y-axis at (0, 2).
Reading left to right, f rises until x = −1 and falls after it: increasing on (−∞, −1), decreasing on (−1, ∞).
solutionReview.answerSummary: Maximum (−1, 4); axis x = −1; x-intercepts (−3, 0) and (1, 0); y-intercept (0, 2); domain (−∞, ∞); range (−∞, 4].
solutionReview.commonError: Writing increasing and decreasing intervals with y-values, such as (−∞, 4).

questions.prompt: The graph shows $f(x)=|x+2|-3$ on the closed interval $-5\le x\le 3$. Find the maximum and minimum values of $f$ on this interval, where each occurs, and the range of $f$ on the interval.

answerFields.label: Maximum value of f on the interval
x-value where the maximum occurs
Minimum value of f on the interval
x-value where the minimum occurs
Range of f on the interval (interval notation)

steps.title: Candidates
steps.instruction: On a closed interval, the maximum and minimum can only occur at an endpoint or at the vertex — and the vertex counts only when it is inside the interval.

steps.title: Evaluate
steps.instruction: Find f at every candidate: both endpoints and the vertex.

steps.title: Compare
steps.instruction: The largest output is the maximum value and the smallest is the minimum value. The range on the interval runs from the minimum to the maximum.

hints: Evaluate f at both endpoints of the interval.
Is the vertex inside the interval? If so, it is a candidate too.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Which points could give the maximum or minimum on a closed interval?

solutionReview.headline: Check the endpoints and the vertex.
reasoning: The vertex x = −2 is inside the interval: f(−2) = −3.
The largest output is 2 (at x = 3) and the smallest is −3 (at x = −2).
solutionReview.answerSummary: Maximum 2 at x = 3; minimum −3 at x = −2; range [−3, 2].
solutionReview.commonError: Checking only the endpoints, which misses the vertex and gives a wrong minimum of 0.

questions.prompt: The graph of $f(x)=|x|$ is shown with five defining points. Graph $g(x)=-\frac{1}{2}|x+2|+3$ by moving each defining point to its image.

steps.title: The mapping rule
steps.instruction: For g(x) = a|x − h| + k, each point (x, y) on f moves to (x + h, a·y + k).

steps.title: x’s lie
steps.instruction: Inside the bars, x + 2 is x − (−2): the graph shifts LEFT 2, so h = −2.

steps.title: y’s tell the truth
steps.instruction: Outside the bars, −½ multiplies every y-value: a reflection across the x-axis and a vertical compression by a factor of ½. Then + 3 shifts the graph up 3.

hints: Map one point at a time: new x = x − 2, new y = −½·y + 3.
Start with the vertex of f. Where must the vertex of g be?

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Which way does x + 2 inside the bars move the graph?

solutionReview.headline: Move every defining point with (x, y) → (x − 2, −½·y + 3).
reasoning: g is f reflected across the x-axis, compressed vertically by a factor of ½, shifted left 2 and up 3.
solutionReview.answerSummary: Vertex (−2, 3); g opens downward and is half as steep as f.
solutionReview.commonError: Shifting right 2 because of the + sign inside the bars.

questions.prompt: Describe every transformation that takes $f(x)=|x|$ to $g(x)=\left|\frac{1}{2}(x-4)\right|-1$.

steps.title: Inside versus outside
steps.instruction: Changes inside the bars act on x, opposite and reciprocal: f(bx) is a horizontal stretch or compression by a factor of 1/|b|. Changes outside act on y, exactly as written.

steps.title: An absolute value shortcut
steps.instruction: Because |bx| = |b|·|x|, the graph of |½(x − 4)| is the same as ½|x − 4|. A horizontal stretch by 2 and a vertical compression by ½ draw the same V, so either description is correct.

steps.title: Reflections
steps.instruction: A negative a reflects the graph across the x-axis. A negative b reflects it across the y-axis — which leaves |x| unchanged, because |−x| = |x|.

hints: Find the shifts first: what value of x makes the inside of the bars zero, and what is added outside?
The factor ½ is inside the bars, so it acts on x: the horizontal scale factor is 1/|b|.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. The factor ½ is inside the bars. What does it change?
options: The horizontal size of the graph
The vertical shift of the graph
scaffold.correct: The horizontal size of the graph

solutionReview.headline: Inside the bars acts on x; outside acts on y.
reasoning: Inside: ½(x − 4) gives a horizontal stretch by a factor of 2 and a shift right 4.
Outside: − 1 shifts the graph down 1. There are no reflections.
Equivalently, |½(x − 4)| = ½|x − 4|: a vertical compression by a factor of ½, right 4, down 1.
solutionReview.answerSummary: Horizontal stretch by 2 (equivalently, vertical compression by ½), right 4, down 1.
solutionReview.commonError: Calling the factor ½ a horizontal compression by ½ — factors inside the bars act reciprocally.

questions.prompt:
Formulate absolute value equations from two different representations.
(A) A regulation size-5 soccer ball must have a circumference within 1 centimeter of 69 centimeters. Let c be a ball’s circumference, in centimeters.
(B) On a number line, the two solutions of an absolute value equation are −7 and 3.

answerFields.label: (A) An absolute value equation whose solutions are the least and greatest allowed circumferences
(A) Least allowed circumference (cm)
(A) Greatest allowed circumference (cm)
(B) The center: the number halfway between −7 and 3
(B) The distance from the center to each solution
(B) An absolute value equation whose solutions are −7 and 3

steps.title: Absolute value is distance
steps.instruction: |x − c| is the distance between x and c. “Within d of c” has boundary values that solve |x − c| = d: the numbers c − d and c + d.

steps.title: From two solutions
steps.instruction: The center c is the midpoint (average) of the two solutions, and d is the distance from the center to either one. Then write |x − c| = d.

steps.title: Watch the sign
steps.instruction: A center of −2 is written |x − (−2)| = |x + 2|.

hints: In (A), the target value is the center and the allowed difference is the distance.
In (B), average the two solutions to find the center; each solution is the same distance from it.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. In |x − c| = d, what does c represent?
options: The distance from the center to each solution
The center, halfway between the two solutions
scaffold.correct: The center, halfway between the two solutions

solutionReview.headline: Absolute value equations model distance from a center.
reasoning: (A) The center is 69 and the distance is 1: |c − 69| = 1, so c = 68 or c = 70.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing |x − 2| = 5 for a center of −2: subtracting a negative center becomes + 2.

questions.prompt: Solve $-3|2x-5|+4=-11$. Isolate the absolute value, decide whether a solution is possible, split the equation into two equations, and check each answer.

steps.title: Isolate first
steps.instruction: Undo the outside operations in reverse order: subtract 4, then divide by −3. Dividing both sides of an EQUATION by a negative number does not change the equal sign.

steps.title: Check the other side
steps.instruction: |A| = d needs d ≥ 0. A negative d means no solution; d = 0 means exactly one solution.

steps.title: Split and solve
steps.instruction: |A| = d becomes A = d or A = −d. Solve both linear equations.

steps.title: Check
steps.instruction: Substitute each answer into the original equation; an answer that fails is extraneous.

hints: Subtract 4 from both sides, then divide both sides by −3.
Once |2x − 5| is alone, the other side tells you how many solutions to expect.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. What is the first move in −3|2x − 5| + 4 = −11?

solutionReview.headline: Isolate, split, solve, check.
reasoning: Solve: x = 5 or x = 0. Both check in the original equation.
solutionReview.commonError: Treating the bars like parentheses and distributing −3 into them.

questions.prompt: Solve $-2|x-4|+7>-3$. Then graph the solution set and write it in interval notation.

steps.title: Isolate — and flip
steps.instruction: Subtract 7, then divide by −2. Dividing both sides of an INEQUALITY by a negative number reverses the symbol.

steps.title: Less than means between (AND)
steps.instruction: |A| < d means −d < A < d: the values within d of the center form one interval.

steps.title: Greater than means outside (OR)
steps.instruction: |A| > d means A < −d or A > d: the values more than d from the center form two rays.

steps.title: Graph and interval notation
steps.instruction: Use open circles and parentheses for < and >; closed circles and brackets for ≤ and ≥.

hints: After subtracting 7, divide both sides by −2 — and reverse the inequality symbol.
Once |x − 4| is alone, decide: is it less than a number (between) or greater than a number (outside)?

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. What happens to > when you divide both sides by −2?

solutionReview.headline: Isolate (reversing the symbol), then write a between statement.
reasoning: Open circles at −1 and 9 with shading between them: (−1, 9).
solutionReview.commonError: Forgetting to reverse the symbol, which gives the OR answer x < −1 or x > 9.

questions.prompt: Solve $|3x+6|-4\ge 5$. Then graph the solution set and write it in interval notation.

steps.title: Isolate
steps.instruction: Add 4 to both sides so the absolute value is alone.

steps.title: Greater than or equal means OR
steps.instruction: |A| ≥ d means A ≤ −d or A ≥ d. Solve each piece, then join them with OR — a union (∪) in interval notation.

hints: Add 4 to both sides so |3x + 6| is alone.
≥ means outside: write two inequalities joined by OR.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Should |3x + 6| ≥ 9 become a between (AND) statement or an outside (OR) statement?

solutionReview.headline: Isolate, then write an outside (OR) statement.
reasoning: Closed circles at −5 and 1, shading outward: (−∞, −5] ∪ [1, ∞).
solutionReview.commonError: Writing the between answer −5 ≤ x ≤ 1 for a ≥ inequality.

questions.prompt: In a playoff game, the DeSoto Eagles made 34 shots for a total of 70 points: free throws (1 point each), two-point field goals (2 points each), and three-point field goals (3 points each). They made 6 more two-point field goals than free throws and three-pointers combined. Let x, y, and z be the numbers of free throws, two-point field goals, and three-point field goals. Write a matrix equation A · X = B for the situation, solve it with technology, and report how many of each shot they made.

steps.title: Define, then translate
steps.instruction: Name what each variable counts. Then write one equation for each fact: how many in all, how many points in all, and how two quantities compare.

steps.title: Standard form
steps.instruction: Move every variable term to the left side: Ax + By + Cz = D. A missing variable has coefficient 0.

steps.title: Matrix equation
steps.instruction: A holds the coefficients (one row per equation), X is the column of variables, and B holds the constants. Technology finds X = A⁻¹B.

hints: One equation counts shots, one counts points, and one compares two-point field goals with the other two kinds of shots.
Which is larger: the number of two-point field goals, or free throws and three-pointers combined? Add 6 to the smaller amount to make the two sides equal.

solutionReview.headline: Translate each fact into one equation, then let technology solve A · X = B.
reasoning: Shots: x + y + z = 34. Points: x + 2y + 3z = 70. Comparison: y = x + z + 6, which is −x + y − z = 6 in standard form.
solutionReview.answerSummary: 6 free throws, 20 two-point field goals, and 8 three-point field goals.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing the comparison as y + 6 = x + z, which makes free throws and three-pointers the larger amount.

questions.prompt: Solve the system by elimination — Gaussian elimination by hand. Eliminate the same variable from two different pairs of equations, solve the resulting 2×2 system, back-substitute, and verify the ordered triple in all three original equations.

steps.title: Plan
steps.instruction: Choose one variable to eliminate. Here y is convenient: equations 1 and 2 have opposite y-coefficients.

steps.title: Two pairs, same variable
steps.instruction: Eliminate the SAME variable twice, using two different pairs of equations, to get a 2×2 system in the other two variables.

steps.title: Back-substitute and verify
steps.instruction: Solve the 2×2 system, substitute into an original equation for the third variable, then check the ordered triple in all three equations.

hints: Adding equations 1 and 2 eliminates y.
To eliminate y using equations 1 and 3, multiply equation 1 by 2 first.

solutionReview.headline: Eliminate y twice, solve the 2×2 system, back-substitute.
reasoning: From x = 9 − 3z: 3(9 − 3z) + 4z = 17, so z = 2 and x = 3.
Equation 1: 3 + y + 2 = 4, so y = −1. (3, −1, 2) checks in all three equations.
solutionReview.commonError: Eliminating y from one pair but a different variable from the other pair, which does not produce a 2×2 system.

questions.prompt: Error analysis: Marcus used technology to solve the system 3x − 2y = 4z − 4, x + 4z = 2y + 16, 2x + y + z = 6. His calculator returned x = −0.25, y = 4.875, z = 1.625, which does not check in the first equation. His matrix equation is already filled in, and two of its rows are wrong. Find his errors, fix A and B, and then solve the system with the matrix calculator.

steps.title: Check the answer first
steps.instruction: A solution must make every original equation true. One that fails tells you the matrix equation is wrong somewhere.

steps.title: Standard form, then copy
steps.instruction: Write each equation as Ax + By + Cz = D before you copy it into a row. A term that crosses the equal sign changes its sign.

steps.title: Fix, solve, check
steps.instruction: Correct the rows that do not match, compute X = A⁻¹B, and check the ordered triple in all three equations.

hints: Before you copy coefficients, every equation must be in standard form: variable terms on the left, the constant on the right.
In the first equation, 4z starts on the right side. When it moves to the left side, what happens to its sign? Compare that with Marcus’s row 1.
In the second equation, 2y starts on the right side. Check the y-coefficient in Marcus’s row 2 the same way.

solutionReview.headline: Marcus copied two equations into A before putting them in standard form.
reasoning: First equation: 3x − 2y = 4z − 4 becomes 3x − 2y − 4z = −4, so row 1 is [3, −2, −4 | −4]. Marcus kept +4 for z.
Second equation: x + 4z = 2y + 16 becomes x − 2y + 4z = 16, so row 2 is [1, −2, 4 | 16]. Marcus kept +2 for y.
Row 3, [2, 1, 1 | 6], was already right. With technology, X = A⁻¹B gives (2, −1, 3).
solutionReview.commonError: Copying a coefficient from the right side of the equal sign without changing its sign.

sections.title: Practice — Independent Mastery (your own version of every problem)

questions.prompt: The graph of an absolute value function f is shown. Analyze its key attributes.
hints: Find the vertex first, then read each attribute from it.
Increasing and decreasing intervals use x-values; the range uses y-values.
attemptFeedback: Locate the vertex: its x-coordinate splits the decreasing and increasing intervals, and its y-coordinate starts the range.

solutionReview.headline: Find the vertex first; every other attribute follows from it.
reasoning: The vertex is ({{h}}, {{k}}) and the V opens upward, so f has a minimum value of {{k}} at x = {{h}}; the axis of symmetry is x = {{h}}.
The x-intercepts ({{x1}}, 0) and ({{x2}}, 0) are each {{d}} units from the axis; the y-intercept is (0, {{yint}}).
f decreases on (−∞, {{h}}) and increases on ({{h}}, ∞).
solutionReview.commonError: Starting the range at the vertex’s x-value instead of its y-value.

questions.prompt: Let $f(x)={{a|coef}}|x {{mh|signed}}| {{k|signed}}$. Find the maximum and minimum values of $f$ on the interval ${{p}}\le x\le {{q}}$, where each occurs, and the range of $f$ on that interval.

answerFields.label: Maximum value of f on the interval
x-value where the maximum occurs
Minimum value of f on the interval
x-value where the minimum occurs
Range of f on the interval (interval notation)

hints: On a closed interval, compare the outputs at both endpoints and at the vertex.
Because a is negative, the vertex is the highest point of the V.
attemptFeedback: Evaluate f at x = {{p}}, at x = {{q}}, and at the vertex x = {{h}}. The largest and smallest of those outputs are the maximum and minimum.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. This V opens downward. Where can its minimum on a closed interval occur?
options: At an endpoint of the interval
scaffold.correct: At an endpoint of the interval

solutionReview.headline: Check the endpoints and the vertex.
reasoning: The vertex ({{h}}, {{k}}) is inside the interval and the V opens down, so the maximum is {{k}} at x = {{h}}.
The smaller endpoint value, {{mn}}, is the minimum, at x = {{xmn}}.
solutionReview.answerSummary: Maximum {{k}} at x = {{h}}; minimum {{mn}} at x = {{xmn}}; range [{{mn}}, {{k}}].
solutionReview.commonError: Assuming the minimum is at the left endpoint — compare both endpoints.

questions.prompt: The graph shows a transformation of $f(x)=|x|$. Find the values of a, h, and k so that the graph is $y=a|x-h|+k$.
hints: The vertex of the V is (h, k).
From the vertex, move 1 unit right and count how far the graph rises or falls: that change is a.
attemptFeedback: Check the sign of a: a V that opens downward has a negative a.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Which point on the graph gives you h and k?
options: The vertex — the corner of the V
scaffold.correct: The vertex — the corner of the V

solutionReview.headline: Read h and k at the vertex, then a from the steepness.
reasoning: The vertex is ({{h}}, {{k}}), so h = {{h}} and k = {{k}}.
One unit right of the vertex, the graph changes by {{a}}, so a = {{a}}.

questions.prompt: Solve the system. Choose substitution or elimination, reduce it to a 2×2 system, back-substitute, and verify the ordered triple.
hints: Look for a variable whose coefficient is 1 or −1 — it is the easiest to eliminate or to solve for.
Eliminate the same variable from two different pairs of equations.
attemptFeedback: Substitute your triple into all three original equations; an equation that fails points to the arithmetic slip.

solutionReview.headline: Eliminate one variable twice, solve the 2×2 system, back-substitute.
reasoning: z has coefficient ±1 in every equation, so eliminating z is efficient: add equations 1 and 3, and add equation 1 to equation 2 after scaling.
Solve the resulting 2×2 system for x and y, then back-substitute for z.
The solution is ({{x0}}, {{y0}}, {{z0}}); it satisfies all three original equations.
solutionReview.commonError: A sign error when subtracting equations — the minus sign must reach every term.

questions.prompt: Write the system as a matrix equation A · X = B — put each equation in standard form first — then solve it with technology: X = A⁻¹ · B.
hints: Move every variable term to the left side of each equation before you write its row of A.
Enter A and B in the calculator, then compute A⁻¹ · B.
attemptFeedback: Check A row by row: each row holds the x-, y-, and z-coefficients of one equation in standard form, with 0 for a missing variable.

solutionReview.headline: Standard form first, then A · X = B, then X = A⁻¹ · B.
reasoning: Rewrite every equation as ax + by + cz = d: move each variable term to the left side and each constant to the right, changing the sign of anything that crosses the equal sign.
Row i of A holds the x-, y-, and z-coefficients of equation i (0 for a missing variable); X is the column (x, y, z); B holds the constants in the same order.
With technology, X = A⁻¹ · B. Read x, y, and z from the column, top to bottom, and check them in the original equations.
solutionReview.answerSummary: The ordered triple (x, y, z) read from A⁻¹ · B.
solutionReview.commonError: Copying coefficients from an equation that is not yet in standard form, so a term moved across the equal sign keeps the wrong sign.

questions.prompt: Honors challenge: solve the equation. The variable appears outside the absolute value too, so check every candidate in the ORIGINAL equation and mark any extraneous solution.

The right side contains x and could be negative
